# Fiat Palio 1.2 Injector Failure: Diagnosing Intermittent Faults and Fuel Efficiency Drops

A non-functioning fuel injector on a Fiat Palio 1.2 (2003) presents a classic case of partial system failure rather than a simple binary "dead or alive" state. Your diagnosis using an engine stethoscope and multimeter is technically sound: zero resistance confirms the internal coil is open, meaning the solenoid cannot actuate to deliver fuel. However, the behavior you are observingâthe check engine light blinking intermittently and the significant drop in mileage when the light is offâreveals how the Engine Control Unit (ECU) handles sensor data and why it compensates differently depending on which cylinder is affected.

The intermittent nature of the warning light is a direct result of the ECU's diagnostic logic. Modern ECUs, even on older 2003 models, do not rely solely on a hard failure to illuminate a lamp. Instead, they monitor injector pulse width and pressure feedback against expected values. When the ECU attempts to fire the second cylinder's injector and detects zero resistance or no current draw, it registers an immediate fault code (typically P0202 for Injector Circuit Malfunction). However, if the wiring harness has a loose ground connection or if the fuel pump relay drops momentarily due to voltage sag, the circuit might briefly re-establish connectivity. This creates a "flashing" condition where the ECU sees the injector work sporadically, triggering the lamp only when the fault is detected again.

The disparity in mileage between the light being on and off stems from how the ECU manages fuel trims. When the warning light is illuminated but the car feels powerful, the ECU is likely running in "Open Loop" or using a learned compensation strategy. Upon detecting the missing injector signal, the ECU may increase the pulse width to the remaining three injectors by 10â20% to maintain overall air-fuel ratio targets. This extra fuel delivery masks the power loss during acceleration but burns significantly more gasoline, which explains why the mileage seems acceptable despite the fault.

Conversely, when the light turns off and mileage plummets, the ECU has likely entered a "Limp Mode" or reverted to a fail-safe strategy because the fault code has cleared from the active monitor list (perhaps due to the intermittent nature of the connection). In this state, the ECU may default to a strict fuel map without the learned enrichment compensation. Without that extra fuel delivery to the healthy cylinders, the engine runs leaner than intended under load. This leads to poor combustion efficiency, rough idling, and drastically reduced fuel economy, even though the car feels like it has "power" because the ECU isn't trying to compensate for the missing cylinder anymore.

From a technical standpoint, replacing the injector is the only viable repair, but you must verify the wiring integrity first. A zero-ohm reading on the coil indicates an open circuit inside the solenoid valve. Before condemning the part, disconnect the fuel rail pressure and check the injector connector for corrosion or broken wires that could mimic a dead injector. If the wiring is sound, the internal armature has likely failed to move due to carbon buildup or electrical burnout.

Addressing this issue via software tuning is generally not recommended on a production vehicle like the Palio. While advanced tuners can disable the cylinder in the ECU map (effectively turning it into a 3-cylinder engine running on all four cylinders), this requires precise fuel mapping to prevent detonation and excessive heat in the remaining cylinders. For most owners, physically replacing the faulty injector with an OEM or high-quality aftermarket unit is the safest path to restoring factory fuel economy and reliability.
